title: Countries, nationalities and languages: je suis canadienne
summary: Say where you are from and where you live: en France, au Canada, aux États-Unis; je suis canadienne; je parle anglais.
focus: Countries with their gender and preposition, nationalities that agree, and languages
content:
## Countries have a gender

Every country is **feminine**, **masculine** or **plural**, and has its article:

| feminine | masculine | plural |
|---|---|---|
| **la France** | **le Canada** | **les États-Unis** |
| **la Belgique** | **le Japon** | **les Pays-Bas** |
| **la Suisse** | **le Sénégal** | **les Philippines** |
| **l'Italie** | **le Maroc** | |

Most countries ending in **-e** are feminine; the others are masculine. A few end in **-e** and are still masculine: **le Mexique**, **le Cambodge**, **le Mozambique**. Before a vowel, **le** and **la** become **l'**: **l'Allemagne** (f), **l'Iran** (m). Country names keep their capital letter.

## In, to and from a country

One little word means both *in* and *to*:

- **en** + a feminine country or one starting with a vowel: **en France**, **en Italie**, **en Iran**
- **au** (à + le) + a masculine country: **au Canada**, **au Japon**
- **aux** (à + les) + a plural country: **aux États-Unis**
- **à** + a city: **à Paris**, **à Montréal**, **à Dakar**

*From* is **venir de**, with the same pattern: **je viens de France**, **d'Italie** (before a vowel), **du Japon** (de + le), **des États-Unis** (de + les), **de Montréal**. To ask, say **Tu viens d'où ?** or **Vous venez d'où ?** (Where are you from?)

## Nationalities and languages

A nationality is an adjective: it agrees, takes **no capital** and, after **être**, no article (**elle est canadienne**).

| masculine | feminine |
|---|---|
| **français** | **française** |
| **canadien** | **canadienne** |
| **américain** | **américaine** |
| **belge** | **belge** |
| **suisse** | **suisse** |

Words already ending in **-e** stay the same. Only the noun for a person has a capital: **un Français**, **une Canadienne**.

Languages are **masculine** and lower-case, often the masculine nationality: **le français**, **l'anglais**. After **parler** they usually drop the article: **Je parle anglais.** Other verbs keep it: **J'étudie l'espagnol.**

## Vivre, habiter and the French-speaking world

| | vivre (to live) |
|---|---|
| je | **vis** |
| tu | **vis** |
| il / elle / on | **vit** |
| nous | **vivons** |
| vous | **vivez** |
| ils / elles | **vivent** |

**Habiter** says where your home is: **J'habite à Lyon.** **Vivre** says that too, and also *to live* in the wider sense: **Elle vit seule.** (She lives alone.)

French is spoken on every continent: **en Belgique**, **en Suisse**, **au Québec** (a province of Canada; the city is **à Québec**), **au Sénégal**, **au Maroc**. More than three hundred million people speak it.

vocabulary.example: La Suisse est un petit pays.
Le français est une langue difficile ?
Nous habitons en France, à Lille.
vocabulary.example_meaning: We live in France, in Lille.

vocabulary.example: Tu voyages aux États-Unis en juillet ?
vocabulary.example_meaning: Are you travelling to the United States in July?

vocabulary.example: Pierre est français et Julie est française.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Pierre is French and Julie is French.

vocabulary.example: Vous venez d'où ? — Je viens du Japon.
vocabulary.example_meaning: Where are you from? — I'm from Japan.

vocabulary.example: Nous vivons à Dakar, au Sénégal.
vocabulary.example_meaning: We live in Dakar, in Senegal.

quiz.prompt: Le Canada is masculine. Complete: Ma cousine habite ___ Canada.
quiz.explanation: A masculine country takes au (à + le): au Canada. En is for feminine countries, à for cities.

quiz.prompt: Ils passent les vacances ___ Italie. (They spend the holidays in Italy.)
quiz.explanation: L'Italie is feminine and starts with a vowel, so it takes en: en Italie.
hints: Feminine countries take a two-letter word.

quiz.prompt: Marie is from Toronto. Marie est ___.
quiz.explanation: The nationality agrees with Marie (-ien becomes -ienne) and, as an adjective, takes no capital: Marie est canadienne.

quiz.prompt: Le Japon is masculine. Je viens ___ Japon. (I come from Japan.)
quiz.explanation: Venir de + le Japon contracts: de + le = du. Je viens du Japon.

quiz.prompt: How do you write 'I speak English' in French?
quiz.explanation: Languages are masculine and lower-case, and after parler they usually take no article: Je parle anglais.

quiz.prompt: Nous ___ à Genève, en Suisse. (vivre: We live in Geneva.)
quiz.explanation: Vivre in the nous form is vivons: nous vivons à Genève.
hints: The stem is viv-, the ending -ons.

quiz.prompt: Le Mexique is masculine even though it ends in -e, so you say 'au Mexique'.
quiz.explanation: Most countries in -e are feminine, but le Mexique (like le Cambodge and le Mozambique) is masculine: au Mexique, du Mexique.
hints: It is one of the exceptions in the first section.

quiz.prompt: Les États-Unis is plural. Mes oncles travaillent ___ États-Unis.
quiz.explanation: A plural country takes aux (à + les): aux États-Unis.

quiz.prompt: 'Elle est Française' is correctly written with a capital F.
quiz.explanation: After être the nationality is an adjective, so it is lower-case: elle est française. Only the noun has a capital: une Française.
hints: Is française an adjective or a noun here?

listening.text: Elle vit à Montréal, au Québec.
listening.meaning: She lives in Montréal, in Quebec.
listening.note: À for the city, au for the province.

listening.meaning: The students come from the United States.
Do you speak German or Italian?

listening.text: Au Sénégal, on parle français et wolof.
listening.meaning: In Senegal, people speak French and Wolof.

listening.text: Ma voisine est belge, mais elle vit en Suisse.
listening.meaning: My neighbour is Belgian, but she lives in Switzerland.
listening.note: Belge is the same in the masculine and the feminine.

guide.tip: Hear the country's article in your head first: la France → en France, le Japon → au Japon, les États-Unis → aux États-Unis.

concept.title: Hear the feminine
concept.markdown: The feminine ending is not only spelling: you can **hear** it. **Français** ends on an *s* you don't say, **française** on a *z* sound. **Canadien** ends in a nasal vowel, **canadienne** in a clear *n*. **Belge** and **suisse** sound the same for everyone.

conversations.title: At the language café
conversations.scenario: Awa, a student from Dakar, meets Lucas from Montréal at a language café in Lyon.

lines.speaker: a
lines.meaning: Good evening! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Je viens du Canada, de Montréal. Et toi ?
lines.meaning: I'm from Canada, from Montréal. And you?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Moi, je suis sénégalaise. Je viens de Dakar.
lines.meaning: I'm Senegalese. I come from Dakar.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Et maintenant, tu vis à Lyon ?
lines.meaning: And now you live in Lyon?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Oui, j'étudie ici. Tu parles anglais ?
lines.meaning: Yes, I'm studying here. Do you speak English?

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Oui, à Montréal, on parle français et anglais.
lines.meaning: Yes, in Montréal people speak French and English.

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Moi, je parle français, anglais et wolof.
lines.meaning: I speak French, English and Wolof.

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Le wolof ? C'est une langue du Sénégal ?
lines.meaning: Wolof? Is that a language from Senegal?

lines.speaker: a
lines.text: Oui ! Et mon frère vit aux États-Unis, à Boston.
lines.meaning: Yes! And my brother lives in the United States, in Boston.
lines.note: aux + a plural country, à + a city

lines.speaker: b
lines.text: Super ! Ma sœur habite en Belgique, à Bruxelles.
lines.meaning: Great! My sister lives in Belgium, in Brussels.

bites.title: Every country has a gender
bites.rule: Feminine (la France), masculine (le Canada) or plural (les États-Unis). Most countries ending in -e are feminine; le Mexique is an exception.
bites.example: La Belgique est un petit pays.

bites.title: En, au, aux, à
bites.rule: En + feminine country or vowel, au + masculine, aux + plural, à + city. Venir de follows: de France, du Japon, des États-Unis.
bites.example_meaning: I live in Canada, in Toronto.

bites.title: Nationalities agree
bites.rule: No capital and no article after être: il est français, elle est française. Belge and suisse never change.
bites.example: Elle est suisse et il est américain.

bites.title: Parler + language
bites.rule: Languages are masculine and lower-case, and take no article after parler: je parle anglais.

sorts.title: En, au or aux?
sorts.why: Feminine countries (and vowels) take en, masculine ones au, plural ones aux.

sorts.title: Il est… or elle est…?
sorts.why: The feminine adds -e (-ien doubles the n: -ienne); a nationality already ending in -e fits both.

spots.why: Le Canada is masculine: au Canada.
Le Japon is masculine: de + le = du.
A plural country takes aux: aux États-Unis.
Paul is a man, so the adjective is masculine: français.
La France is feminine: de France, not du.

builds.meaning: The students live in the United States.
